title: No Size-Preserving Amplification with Quantum Advice
abstract: Marriott and Watrous showed that quantum Merlin--Arthur games admit generic error reduction without increasing witness size [Computational Complexity, 2005]. In this work, we show that this state-size-preserving amplification property does not hold for polynomial-time quantum computation with quantum advice. In particular, we present decision problems for which even a vanishing additive error reduction requires longer advice. More precisely, for every polynomially bounded advice length $m(n)\geq n^4$ and every error bound $\varepsilon(n)$ that stays below $1/2$ by at least an inverse polynomial, there is a positive function $δ$ with $δ(n)=O\bigl(\min\{(\log m/m)^{1/4},\ \sqrt{\log m/m}\,/(1/2-\varepsilon(n))\}\bigr)$ such that $\mathsf{BQP}_{\varepsilon}/\mathsf{q}m \subsetneq \mathsf{BQP}_{\varepsilon + δ}/\mathsf{q}m$; for constant $\varepsilon$ the gap is $O(\sqrt{\log m/m})$. Here, $\mathsf{BQP}_\varepsilon/\mathsf{q}m$ is the class of languages recognizable with error at most $\varepsilon(n)$ by a polynomial-time quantum algorithm with an $m(n)$-qubit advice state that only depends on the input length $n$. We show this by proving a stronger separation $\mathsf{P}_{\varepsilon+δ}/\mathsf{r} m \not\subset \mathsf{BQP}_{\varepsilon}/\mathsf{q} m$, where $\mathsf{P}_{\varepsilon}/\mathsf{r}m$ is the class of languages recognizable with error at most $\varepsilon(n)$ by a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm with an $m(n)$-bit advice string sampled from a distribution that depends only on $n$.
summary: This paper proves a significant limitation in quantum computation theory by showing that error reduction in quantum algorithms with fixed-size quantum advice cannot be arbitrarily small. It establishes a quantitative separation between complexity classes $	ext{BQP}_{\epsilon}/	ext{q}^m$ and $	ext{BQP}_{\epsilon+\delta}/	ext{q}^m$, using sophisticated tools from coding theory and information theory.
main_problem: The paper investigates whether the size-preserving amplification property, known for quantum Merlin-Arthur games, holds for quantum computation utilizing quantum advice.
main_result: It proves that this size-preserving amplification fails for quantum advice, demonstrating a strict separation between complexity classes $	ext{BQP}_{\epsilon}/	ext{q}^m$ and $	ext{BQP}_{\epsilon+\delta}/	ext{q}^m$.
method: The proof uses advanced techniques combining diagonalization arguments, random access coding theory (Toeplitz codes), and entropy analysis derived from information theory bounds.
model_or_system: The model involves computational complexity classes defined by polynomial-time quantum algorithms ($	ext{BQP}$) that receive an advice state ($	ext{q}^m$) of fixed size $m(n)$ depending only on the input length $n$.
key_observables: The separation gap $\delta(n)$ quantifying the required increase in error tolerance to establish the inclusion failure.
important_parameters: Advice length $m(n) \geq n^4$, error bounds $\epsilon(n)$ staying below $1/2$ by an inverse polynomial, and the separation gap $\delta(n) = O(\min\{(\log m/m)^{1/4}, \sqrt{\log m/m/(1/2-\epsilon(n))}\})$.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the existence of polynomially bounded advice length $m(n)$ and that the error bound $\epsilon(n)$ is sufficiently far from $1/2$.
paper_structure: The paper builds from fundamental entropy bounds ($\Phi(\epsilon, \eta)$) and random access code theorems (Nayak's bound) to construct specific languages $L(k)_R$. It then uses these constructions to prove lower and upper bounds, culminating in the separation results between $	ext{P}_{\epsilon+\delta}/	ext{r}^m$ and $	ext{BQP}_{\epsilon}/	ext{q}^m$.
why_interesting: This work establishes fundamental limitations on how much error reduction can be achieved in quantum computation when the advice state size is fixed, which has implications for the theoretical limits of quantum computation models.
